criteria.evidence_quote: The compensation point is 75 micromol photons/m^2/s, the light intensity where photosynthesis and respiration are perfectly balanced so there is no net gas exchange.

criteria.evidence_quote: Doubling the CO2 concentration would actually increase the light compensation point.

criteria.minimum_fix: Compensation point decreases; more CO2 increases Calvin cycle rate at each light level so lower light intensity is needed to offset respiration.

criteria.evidence_quote: Light energy absorbed at photosystem II excites electrons that travel down the electron transport chain to photosystem I, and the energy released pumps protons from the thylakoid lumen into the stroma, creating a gradient. The protons then flow back through ATP synthase from the stroma into the lumen, and this flow drives the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
criteria.decision_explanation: The response correctly includes light excitation at PSII and electron flow through the electron transport chain, but the proton gradient and ATP synthase direction are reversed, so only partial credit is warranted.

criteria.evidence_quote: The first labeled organic compound would be 3-phosphoglycerate, since carbon fixation attaches CO2 to RuBP and the unstable intermediate splits into two 3-PGA molecules. When the light is turned off, RuBP concentration would actually increase over the next two minutes, because the Calvin cycle immediately stops running without light, so RuBisCO can no longer consume RuBP and it builds up in the stroma while the ATP and NADPH already present are used up elsewhere.
